div.head: Section 103
div.p: Socrates. Son of Clinias, I think you are wondering why I, who became your first lover, am the only one who has not gone away now that the others have stopped; and why the others made themselves troublesome to you by talking with you, while I, for so many years, have not even addressed you. The cause of this has not been human, but a certain divine opposition, whose power you will learn later. But now, since it no longer opposes me, I have approached you in this way; and I am hopeful that hereafter it will not oppose me either. During this time, then, I have quite closely observed, as I watched, how you behaved toward your lovers. For though many of them came, and high-spirited men too, there was not one who did not flee after being overpowered by your pride.

div.head: Section 104
div.p: Socrates. I want to go through the reason by which you have come to think so highly of yourself. You say that you are in need of no human being for anything; for what belongs to you is so great that you need no one, beginning with your body and ending with your soul. You think, first, that you are the fairest and tallest, and indeed it is clear for anyone to see that in this you are not lying; next, that you are of one of the most distinguished families in your city here; that on your father's side you have very many and excellent friends and kinsmen, who would serve you if you needed anything, and that those on your mother's side are no worse or fewer. But greater than all the things I have mentioned, you think, is the power you possess in Pericles son of Xanthippus, whom your father left as guardian over you and your brother. He is able to do whatever he wishes not only in this city, but in all Greece, and among many great peoples of the barbarians. I will add, too, that you are among the rich; but you seem to me to pride yourself least on that. Boasting of all these things, you have prevailed over your lovers, and they, being inferior, were overcome; and this has not escaped you. From this I know well that you wonder what I can possibly be thinking, that I do not depart from my love, and what hope I have that makes me remain when the others have fled.

Alcibiades. And perhaps, Socrates, you do not know that you only just forestalled me. For I had it in mind to come to you first and ask you these very things: what you want, and looking toward what hope you bother me, always most carefully present wherever I may be. For in truth I wonder what this business of yours is, and I would very gladly learn it.
Socrates. Then you will listen to me eagerly, as is likely, if indeed, as you say, you desire to know what I have in mind; and I speak as to someone who will listen and wait.
Alcibiades. Certainly; but speak.
Socrates. Look then; for it would not be surprising if, just as I began with difficulty, so I should also stop with difficulty.
Alcibiades. My good man, speak; for I shall listen.

div.head: Section 105
div.p:
Socrates. Then it must be said. Now it is hard for a lover to approach a man who is not inferior to his lovers; nevertheless I must dare to state my thought. For if I saw you, Alcibiades, content with the things I just went through and thinking that you ought to spend your life in them, I would long ago have been released from my love,
at least as I persuade myself. But now I will lay other thoughts of yours as a charge against you yourself, by which you will also know that I have continued all along to keep my mind fixed on you. For I think that if one of the gods were to say to you, "Alcibiades, do you wish to live having what you now have, or to die at once if it will not be possible for you to acquire greater things?" you would choose, I think, to die. But I will tell you now on what hope you are living. You suppose that if you quickly come before the Athenian people, and this will happen within very few days, then, once you have come forward, you will show the Athenians that you deserve to be honored as neither Pericles nor anyone else who has ever lived; and that, having shown this, you will have the greatest power in the city. And if you are greatest here, you will be greatest among the other Greeks too, and not only among Greeks, but also among the barbarians, all who live on the same continent as we do. And if this same god were then to tell you that you must rule here in Europe, but that it would not be possible for you to cross into Asia or to lay your hand on affairs there, I think you would again be unwilling to live on these terms alone, unless you could fill nearly all human beings, one might say, with your name and your power. And I think you believe that no one except Cyrus and Xerxes has ever been worthy of mention. That you have this hope, then, I know well and am not guessing. Perhaps, then, since you know that I am telling the truth, you might say, "What, then, Socrates, does this have to do with the matter? You said you would tell me why you do not leave me." I will indeed tell you, dear son of Clinias and Deinomache. For it is impossible for all these thoughts of yours to reach their fulfillment without me; so great a power do I think I have over your affairs and over you. That is why I think the god has so long prevented me from conversing with you, and I was waiting until he allowed it. For just as you have hopes of showing the city that you are worth everything to it, and once you have shown that, of being able to do almost anything at once, so I too hope to have the greatest power with you, after showing that I am worth everything to you, and that neither guardian nor kinsman nor anyone else is capable of handing over to you the power you desire except me, with the god, however. When you were younger, then, and before you were filled with so great a hope, as it seems to me, the god did not allow me to converse with you, so that I would not
converse in vain. But now he has let me; for now you would listen to me.

div.head: Section 106
div.p: Alcibiades. You seem to me, Socrates, much more strange now that you have begun to speak than when you followed me in silence, although even then you looked strange enough. So, whether I have these things in mind or not, you have evidently made up your mind, and if I deny it, it will be to no advantage in persuading you. Very well then: if I indeed intend these things most of all, how will they come about through you, and why without you could they not happen? Can you explain?

Socrates. Are you asking if I have some long speech to give, the sort you are accustomed to hearing? For my way is not like that: but I think I could show you that these things are so, if you are willing to do me just one small service.
Alcibiades. Well, if the service you speak of is not a difficult one, I am willing.
Socrates. Does it seem difficult to answer questions?
Alcibiades. Not difficult.
Socrates. Then answer.
Alcibiades. Ask.
Socrates. Then I ask you under the assumption that you intend the things I say you intend?
Alcibiades. Let it be so, if you wish, so that I may know what you will say.

Socrates. Come then: you intend, as I say, to step forward to advise the Athenians within a short time. If, therefore, as you were about to step onto the platform, I should grab hold of you and ask: "Alcibiades, since the Athenians are planning to deliberate, what is the subject about which you stand up to advise? Is it about things which you know better than they do?" What would you answer?
Alcibiades. I would say, I suppose, about things which I know better than they do.
Socrates. Then concerning the things you happen to know, you are a good advisor.
Alcibiades. How could I not be?
Socrates. Do you know anything except what you have learned from others or found out yourself?
Alcibiades. What else could there be?
Socrates. Is there any way you could have ever learned or found out anything without being willing either to learn it or to seek it out yourself?
Alcibiades. There is not.
Socrates. What then? Would you have been willing to seek out or learn what you thought you already knew?
Alcibiades. No, indeed.
Socrates. So for the things you now happen to know, was there a time when you did not think you knew them?
Alcibiades. Necessarily.

Socrates. But I know pretty much what you have learned. If something has escaped my notice, tell me. For as far as my memory goes, you learned your letters, how to play the lyre, and how to wrestle; you did not wish to learn to play the flute. These are the things you know, unless perhaps you have learned something without my noticing—which I suppose you have not, since you have gone neither out by night nor by day from your house.
Alcibiades. But I have not attended any other classes than these.

div.head: Section 107
div.p: Socrates. Will you then, when the Athenians are deliberating about letters, how they should write correctly, stand up to advise them then?
Alcibiades. By Zeus, not I.
Socrates. Well, when they deliberate about striking notes on the lyre?
Alcibiades. By no means.
Socrates. And they are not accustomed to deliberating about wrestling holds in the assembly, either.
Alcibiades. Certainly not.
Socrates. When, then, are they deliberating about what? For surely not when they deliberate about house-building.
Alcibiades. No, indeed.
Socrates. For a builder will advise better than you about these things.
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Nor when they deliberate about divination?
Alcibiades. No.
Socrates. For a diviner again is better at this than you.
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Whether he is small or large, beautiful or ugly, and furthermore whether he is of noble or common birth.
Alcibiades. How could he not be?
Socrates. For advice, I suppose, comes from the one who knows about each thing, not from the one who is rich.
Alcibiades. How could it not?

Socrates. And whether the advisor is poor or rich, it will make no difference to the Athenians when they deliberate concerning the affairs in the city, such as how they might be healthy; but they will seek a physician to be the advisor.
Alcibiades. Naturally.
Socrates. When they are looking into what, then, will you stand up as one who will give correct advice?
Alcibiades. When they are deliberating about their own affairs, Socrates.
Socrates. Do you mean about shipbuilding, what sort of ships they ought to build?
Alcibiades. Not I, Socrates.
Socrates. For I suppose you do not know how to build ships. Is that the reason, or something else?
Alcibiades. No, that is the reason.
Socrates. But about what sort of their own affairs do you mean, when they deliberate?
Alcibiades. When they deliberate about war, Socrates, or about peace, or some other of the city's affairs.
Socrates. Do you mean when they deliberate with whom they ought to make peace, and with whom to go to war, and in what manner?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And they must do it with those with whom it is better?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And at the time when it is better?
Alcibiades. Certainly.
Socrates. And for as long a time as is better?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. If then the Athenians were deliberating with whom they ought to wrestle, and with whom to engage in close combat, and in what manner, would you advise them better, or the wrestling-master?
Alcibiades. The wrestling-master, I suppose.

Socrates. Can you then say what the wrestling-master would look to in advising them with whom they must wrestle and with whom not, and when, and in what manner? I mean something like this: must they wrestle with those with whom it is better, or not?
Alcibiades. Yes.

div.head: Section 108
div.p: Socrates. And also as many times as is better?
Alcibiades. As many.
Socrates. And also at the time when it is better?
Alcibiades. Certainly.
Socrates. But must one who is singing also sometimes play the lyre to accompany the song, and step in time?
Alcibiades. Yes, he must.
Socrates. Then at the time when it is better?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And as many times as is better?
Alcibiades. I agree.

Socrates. What then? Since you named "better" in both cases, both in playing the lyre to accompany the song and in wrestling, what do you call the "better" in playing the lyre? Just as I call the "better" in wrestling "gymnastic", what do you call the former?
Alcibiades. I don't understand.
Socrates. But try to imitate me. For I answered, I suppose, that it is that which is always correct; and surely what is according to the art is correct, is it not?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And the art was gymnastic, wasn't it?
Alcibiades. How could it not be?
Socrates. And I said that the "better" in wrestling is gymnastic.
Alcibiades. Yes, you did say that.
Socrates. And didn't I speak well?
Alcibiades. It seems so to me.

Socrates. Come then, you too—for it would be fitting for you too, I suppose, to converse well—tell me first, what is the art by which one plays the lyre and sings and steps correctly? What is the whole thing called? Are you not yet able to say?
Alcibiades. No, indeed.
Socrates. Try it this way: who are the goddesses whose art it is?
Alcibiades. Do you mean the Muses, Socrates?
Socrates. I do. See then: what name does the art derive from them?
Alcibiades. You seem to mean music.

Socrates. I do mean that. What then is the thing done correctly according to this art? Just as in the other case I told you that what is according to the art correctly is gymnastic, what do you say it is here? How is it done?
Alcibiades. Musically, it seems to me.

Socrates. You speak well. Come then, what do you name the "better" in making war and the "better" in being at peace? Just as in the other cases you called the "better" thing, on the one hand, more musical, and on the other, more gymnastic; try to say what the "better" is here too.
Alcibiades. But I have no idea at all.

div.head: Section 109
div.p: Socrates. But surely it is a shame if someone should listen to you speaking and advising about foods, saying that this is better than that, both now and in this quantity, and then were to ask: "What do you mean by 'better', Alcibiades?", and concerning these things you would be able to say that it means the more healthy, although you do not pretend to be a physician; but concerning a subject in which you pretend to be knowledgeable and will stand up to advise as one who knows, if you are asked about this and are unable to say, will you not be ashamed, as it seems you are? Or will it not appear shameful?
Alcibiades. Very much so.
Socrates. Consider then and be eager to say: to what does the "better" tend, in being at peace and in making war with those with whom one ought?
Alcibiades. But though I consider it, I cannot conceive of it.
Socrates. And you don't even know, when we wage war, what complaint we make against each other when we enter into war, and what we name the thing we enter into it for?
Alcibiades. I do; we say that we have been deceived in some way, or forced, or robbed.
Socrates. Hold on: how do we suffer each of these things? Try to say what difference there is between suffering them in this way or in that way.
Alcibiades. Do you mean by "this way", Socrates, justly or unjustly?
Socrates. Exactly that.
Alcibiades. But surely this differs in the whole and entirely.
Socrates. What then? To which sort of people will you advise the Athenians to make war, to those who act unjustly or to those who do what is just?
Alcibiades. You ask a terrible question; for even if someone were to intend that one must make war against those who do what is just, he would never admit it.
Socrates. For that is not lawful, as it seems.
Alcibiades. No, indeed; nor does it seem to be noble.
Socrates. Therefore you too will make your speeches directed toward justice?
Alcibiades. Necessarily.

Socrates. Does it not happen then that the "better" about which I just asked—whether to make war or not, and with whom one ought and with whom not, and when and when not—happens to be the more just? Or is it not so?
Alcibiades. It appears so.

Socrates. How then, dear Alcibiades? Have you escaped your own notice not knowing this, or have you escaped my notice learning it and attending the school of a teacher who taught you to distinguish the more just and the more unjust? And who is he? Tell me too, so that you may introduce me to him as a pupil.
Alcibiades. You are joking, Socrates.
Socrates. No, by the god of friendship, yours and mine, whom I would least of all swear by falsely! But if you have one, tell me who he is.
Alcibiades. And what if I don't? Would you not think that I could otherwise know about what is just and unjust?
Socrates. Yes, if you discovered it.
Alcibiades. But do you not think I could discover it?
Socrates. Very much so, if you searched.
Alcibiades. Then do you not think I would search?
Socrates. I do, if you thought you did not know.
Alcibiades. And was there not a time when I was in that state?

div.head: Section 110
div.p: Socrates. You speak well. Can you tell me, then, the time when you did not think you knew the just and the unjust things? Come now, were you searching a year ago and did you not think you knew? Or did you think you knew? And answer truthfully, so that our conversations may not be in vain.
Alcibiades. But I thought I knew.
Socrates. And in the third year, and the fourth, and the fifth, was it not so?
Alcibiades. Yes, it was.
Socrates. But surely before that you were a child, weren't you?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Then I know well that at that time you thought you knew.
Alcibiades. How do you know well?

Socrates. Often I used to hear you at the schoolmasters' when you were a child, and elsewhere, and whenever you were playing knucklebones or any other game, not speaking as if you were in perplexity about just and unjust things, but speaking very loudly and confidently about whichever of the boys you happened to be dealing with, saying that he was wicked and unjust, and that he was acting unjustly; or am I not speaking the truth?
Alcibiades. But what was I supposed to do, Socrates, whenever someone acted unjustly toward me?
Socrates. If you happened to be ignorant of whether you were being treated unjustly or not at that time, you mean, what ought you to do?
Alcibiades. By Zeus, I was not ignorant, but I knew clearly that I was being treated unjustly.
Socrates. You thought you understood, it seems, even when you were a child, the just and unjust things.
Alcibiades. Yes, I did; and I understood them too.
Socrates. In what time did you discover them? For surely it was not in the time when you thought you knew them.
Alcibiades. No, indeed.
Socrates. When, then, did you think you were ignorant? Consider; for you will not find this time.
Alcibiades. By Zeus, Socrates, I cannot say.
Socrates. Then you do not know these things by having discovered them.
Alcibiades. It appears not at all.

div.head: Section 111
div.p: Alcibiades. For example, I learned to speak Greek from them, and I could not name my teacher, but I refer to the same people whom you say are not serious teachers.
Socrates. But, my noble friend, in this at least the many are good teachers, and they would justly be praised for their teaching.
Alcibiades. Why is that?
Socrates. Because they have regarding these things what good teachers ought to have.
Alcibiades. What do you mean by this?
Socrates. Do you not know that those who intend to teach anything must first know it themselves? Or is it not so?
Alcibiades. How could it not be?
Socrates. And must not those who know agree with each other and not differ?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. But in the things in which they differ, will you say that they know them?
Alcibiades. No, indeed.
Socrates. How then could they be teachers of these things?
Alcibiades. By no means.

Socrates. What then? Do the many seem to you to differ about what sort of thing a stone or wood is? And if you ask anyone, do they not agree on the same things, and do they not reach for the same things whenever they wish to take a stone or wood? And similarly with all such things; for I pretty much understand that to know how to speak Greek is what you mean by this, is it not?
Alcibiades. Yes.

Socrates. Do they not then, as we said, agree with each other and with themselves privately concerning these things, and publicly the cities do not dispute with one another, some saying these things and others saying different ones?
Alcibiades. No, they do not.
Socrates. Naturally, then, they would be good teachers of these things.
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. If, therefore, we should wish to make someone know about them, we would rightly send him to the teaching of these many?
Alcibiades. Very much so.
Socrates. What if we wished to know not only what sort of things men or horses are, but also which of them are good runners and which are not, would the many still be capable of teaching this?
Alcibiades. No, indeed.
Socrates. And is it a sufficient proof to you that they do not know and are not genuine teachers of these things, since they do not agree with themselves about them?
Alcibiades. It is to me.
Socrates. What if we wished to know not only what sort of things men are, but what sort are healthy or diseased, would the many be capable teachers for us?
Alcibiades. No, indeed.
Socrates. And it would be a proof to you that they are poor teachers of these things, if you saw them differing?
Alcibiades. It would to me.

div.head: Section 112
div.p: Socrates. What then now? Concerning just and unjust men and affairs, do the many seem to you to agree with themselves or with each other?
Alcibiades. Least of all, by Zeus, Socrates.
Socrates. What then? Do they differ most of all about them?
Alcibiades. Very much so.
Socrates. I suppose you have never seen or heard of men differing so vehemently about healthy and unhealthy things that they fight and kill each other because of them.
Alcibiades. No, indeed.

Socrates. But concerning the just and unjust things, I know well that even if you have not seen it, you have at least heard of it from many others and from Homer; for you have heard both the Odyssey and the Iliad.
Alcibiades. Assuredly, I suppose, Socrates.
Socrates. Are not these poems about a difference concerning just and unjust things?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And the battles and the deaths occurred because of this difference both for the Achaeans and the other Trojans, and for the suitors of Penelope and Odysseus.
Alcibiades. You speak the truth.

Socrates. And I think also for those who died at Tanagra, both Athenians and Lacedaemonians and Boeotians, and those later at Coronea, among whom your father Clinias died too, the difference was about nothing else than the just and the unjust that caused the deaths and the battles, was it not?
Alcibiades. You speak the truth.
Socrates. Shall we say then that these people know the things about which they differ so vehemently that in disputing with one another they inflict the ultimate extremes upon themselves?
Alcibiades. It appears not.
Socrates. Do you then refer to such teachers, whom you yourself agree do not know?
Alcibiades. It seems so.
Socrates. How then is it likely that you know the just and the unjust things, about which you wander so much and appear neither to have learned from anyone nor to have discovered yourself?
Alcibiades. From what you say, it is not likely.
Socrates. Do you see again that you did not speak well in this, Alcibiades?
Alcibiades. In what?
Socrates. That you say that I am saying these things.
Alcibiades. What? Are you not saying that I know nothing about the just and the unjust things?
Socrates. Not at all.
Alcibiades. But am I?
Socrates. Yes.
Alcibiades. How so?
Socrates. You will know in this way. If I ask you about one and two, which is more, you will say that the two are?
Alcibiades. I will.
Socrates. By how much?
Alcibiades. By one.
Socrates. Which of us then is the one who says that the two is more than the one by one?
Alcibiades. I am.
Socrates. Was I not asking, and you answering?
Alcibiades. Yes.

div.head: Section 113
div.p: Socrates. Concerning these things, then, do I appear to be the one speaking, who asks the questions, or you, who answer?
Alcibiades. I do.
Socrates. And what if I ask what the letters of 'Socrates' are, and you say them, which is the one speaking?
Alcibiades. I am.
Socrates. Come then, say it in a word: whenever there is a question and an answer, which is the one speaking, the questioner or the answerer?
Alcibiades. The answerer, it seems to me, Socrates.
Socrates. Was I not the questioner continuously just now?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And you the answerer?
Alcibiades. Very much so.
Socrates. What then? Which of us has spoken the things that were said?
Alcibiades. It appears, Socrates, from what has been agreed, that I have.

Socrates. Was it not said concerning just and unjust things that the beautiful Alcibiades, the son of Clinias, did not know them, but thought he did, and was intending to go to the assembly to advise the Athenians about things he knows nothing about? Was it not this?
Alcibiades. It appears so.

Socrates. The saying of Euripides then applies, Alcibiades: you run the risk of having heard these things from yourself, not from me, nor am I the one saying them, but you, and you blame me in vain. And indeed you speak well. For it is a mad undertaking that you have in mind to attempt, my excellent friend: to teach what you do not know, having neglected to learn.

Alcibiades. I think, Socrates, that the Athenians and the other Greeks seldom deliberate about whether things are more just or more unjust; for they think such things are obvious, and so letting them go they consider which will be advantageous to do. For I think the just and the advantageous are not the same, but it has profited many to have committed great injustices, and for others, I suppose, who have done just things, it has brought no advantage.

Socrates. What then? Even if the just things happen to be as different as possible from the advantageous, surely you do not again think that you know these things that are advantageous to human beings, and why?
Alcibiades. What prevents it, Socrates? Unless you are going to ask me again from whom I learned it or how I discovered it myself.

div.head: Section 114
div.p: Socrates. What a thing you do. If you say something incorrectly, and it happens to be possible to refute it by the very same argument as before, you think you must hear some new proofs and different arguments, as if the previous ones were worn-out little garments, and you would no longer put them on, unless someone brings you a clean and unsoiled proof. But I, letting go your sallies of speech, will ask you no less: from where did you learn to know the advantageous things, and who is the teacher, and all those things I asked before, I ask in a single question? But clearly you will arrive at the same point and will not be able to show either that you know the advantageous things by having discovered them or by having learned them. But since you are dainty and would no longer gladly taste the same argument, I will let this go, whether you know or not what is advantageous to the Athenians; but whether the just and the advantageous are the same or different, why have you not proven it? If you wish, ask me just as I asked you, or if you prefer, go through it yourself by yourself in a speech.
Alcibiades. But I do not know if I would be able, Socrates, to go through it with you.
Socrates. But, my good friend, consider me to be the assembly and the people; and even there you will have to persuade each one individually. Is it not so?
Alcibiades. Yes.

Socrates. Is it not the property of the same person to be able to persuade one individually and many together about whatever he knows, just as the schoolmaster persuades one individually about letters, and also many?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Will not the same person also persuade one and many about number?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And this will be the one who knows, the arithmetician?
Alcibiades. Very much so.
Socrates. Therefore, those things which you are able to persuade many of, you can also persuade one of?
Alcibiades. It is likely.
Socrates. And these are clearly the things that you know.
Alcibiades. Yes.

Socrates. Does the orator in the assembly differ from the one in a gathering such as this only in this much: that the one persuades them all gathered together of the same things, while the other does so one by one?
Alcibiades. It is likely.
Socrates. Come now, since it appears to be the property of the same person to persuade many and one, practice on me and try to show that the just is sometimes not advantageous.
Alcibiades. You are arrogant, Socrates.
Socrates. Now at least, out of arrogance, I am going to persuade you of the very opposite of what you are unwilling to persuade me.
Alcibiades. Speak then.
Socrates. Only answer the questions asked.
Alcibiades. No, but you yourself speak.
Socrates. What? Do you not wish to be persuaded as much as possible?
Alcibiades. Assuredly, I suppose.
Socrates. If you say that these things are so, would you not be most persuaded?
Alcibiades. It seems so to me.
Socrates. Then answer; and if you do not hear from yourself that the just and the advantageous are the same, do not believe anyone else who says it.
Alcibiades. No, I must answer; for I think I shall suffer no harm.

div.head: Section 115
div.p: Socrates. For you are prophetic. Tell me: do you say that some just things are advantageous, while some are not?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. What then? Are some of them beautiful, and some not?
Alcibiades. How do you mean this?
Socrates. Has anyone ever seemed to you to act basely, yet justly?
Alcibiades. Not to me.
Socrates. But are all just things also beautiful?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. What again about beautiful things? Are they all good, or some good and some not?
Alcibiades. I think, Socrates, that some beautiful things are bad.
Socrates. And also that some base things are good?
Alcibiades. Yes.

Socrates. Do you mean things such as this: many who have come to the aid of a comrade or relative in war have received wounds and died, while those who did not help, though they ought to have, came away healthy?
Alcibiades. Very much so.
Socrates. You say that such aid is beautiful in respect to the attempt to save those whom one ought to save, and this is courage, is it not?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. But it is bad in respect to the deaths and wounds, isn't it?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Are not courage and death different things?
Alcibiades. Very much so.
Socrates. Therefore, helping one's friends is not beautiful and bad in the same respect?
Alcibiades. It appears not.

Socrates. See then if, insofar as it is beautiful, it is also good, just as it is here. For you agreed that the aid was beautiful in respect to courage; consider this itself, then: is courage good or bad? Consider it this way: which would you choose to have, good things or bad?
Alcibiades. Good things.
Socrates. And the greatest goods most of all?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And you would least of all choose to be deprived of such things?
Alcibiades. How could I not?
Socrates. What then do you say about courage? For how much would you choose to be deprived of it?
Alcibiades. I would not even accept life if I were a coward.
Socrates. Cowardice, then, seems to you to be the extreme of evils.
Alcibiades. To me it does.
Socrates. On a par with dying, as it seems.
Alcibiades. I agree.
Socrates. Are not life and courage most opposed to death and cowardice?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And would you most of all wish to have the former, and least of all the latter?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Is this because you think the former are the best, and the latter the worst?
Alcibiades. Very much so.
Socrates. Then you consider courage to be among the best things, and death among the worst.

div.head: Section 116
div.p: Alcibiades. I do.
Socrates. Therefore, in regard to helping friends in war, insofar as it is beautiful—in respect to the good action of courage—you called it beautiful?
Alcibiades. I appear to have done so.
Socrates. But in respect to the bad action of death, you called it bad?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Thus it is right to address each of the actions in this way: if insofar as it works evil you call it bad, then insofar as it works good it must be called good.
Alcibiades. It seems so to me.
Socrates. And insofar as it is good, it is beautiful, and insofar as it is bad, it is base?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. By saying that aid to friends in war is beautiful but bad, you are saying nothing different than if you addressed it as good but bad.
Alcibiades. You seem to me to speak the truth, Socrates.
Socrates. Therefore nothing beautiful, insofar as it is beautiful, is bad, nor is anything base, insofar as it is base, good.
Alcibiades. It appears not.
Socrates. Consider this further in this way: whoever acts beautifully, does he not also act well?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And are not those who act well happy?
Alcibiades. How could they not be?
Socrates. Are they not happy through the possession of good things?
Alcibiades. Most certainly.
Socrates. And they possess these things by acting well and beautifully?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Therefore acting well is good?
Alcibiades. How could it not be?
Socrates. Is not good action beautiful?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Then the beautiful and the good have once again appeared to us to be the same.
Alcibiades. It appears so.
Socrates. Whatever we find to be beautiful, therefore, we shall also find to be good by this argument at least.
Alcibiades. Necessarily.
Socrates. What then? Are good things advantageous or not?
Alcibiades. Advantageous.
Socrates. Do you remember how we agreed about just things?
Alcibiades. I think we agreed that those who do just things necessarily do beautiful things.
Socrates. And that those who do beautiful things do good things?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And that good things are advantageous?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Therefore just things, Alcibiades, are advantageous.
Alcibiades. It seems so.
Socrates. What then? Are you not the one saying these things, and I the one asking?
Alcibiades. I appear to be, as it seems.

Socrates. If then someone stands up to advise either the Athenians or the Peparethians, thinking he knows what is just and unjust, and says that just things are sometimes bad, would you not do anything else but laugh at him, since you yourself happen to be saying that just and advantageous things are the same?

Alcibiades. But by the gods, Socrates, I do not even know what I am saying, but I seem to be in a wholly strange condition; for sometimes things seem one way to me when you question me, and sometimes another way.
Socrates. And then do you not know what this condition is, my friend?
Alcibiades. Very much so.

Socrates. Do you suppose that if someone were to ask you whether you have two eyes or three, and two hands or four, or anything else of the sort, you would sometimes answer one thing and sometimes another, or always the same?

div.head: Section 117
div.p: Alcibiades. I am already afraid for myself, but I suppose I would say the same things.
Socrates. Is this because you know? Is that the cause?
Alcibiades. I suppose so.
Socrates. Clearly then, concerning the things about which you involuntarily answer contrary things, you do not know about them.
Alcibiades. It is likely.

Socrates. And in answering about just and unjust things, beautiful and base things, bad and good things, advantageous and non-advantageous things, do you not say you are wandering? Is it not then clear that you wander because of not knowing about them?
Alcibiades. To me it is.
Socrates. Is it then like this: whenever someone does not know a thing, must his soul necessarily wander concerning this?
Alcibiades. How could it not?
Socrates. What then? Do you know the way in which you will ascend to heaven?
Alcibiades. By Zeus, I do not.
Socrates. Does your opinion wander concerning these things?
Alcibiades. No, indeed.
Socrates. Do you know the cause, or shall I tell you?
Alcibiades. Tell me.
Socrates. It is because, my friend, not knowing it, you do not think you know it.
Alcibiades. How do you mean this again?

Socrates. Consider it with me together. The things you do not know, but you recognize that you do not know them, do you wander about such things? Just as concerning the preparation of food you surely know that you do not know?
Alcibiades. Very much so.
Socrates. Do you then form opinions yourself concerning these things about how one must prepare them and so wander, or do you leave it to the one who knows?
Alcibiades. In that way.

Socrates. What if you were sailing in a ship, would you form opinions about whether one must draw the tiller inwards or outwards, and because you do not know, would you wander, or would you leave it to the pilot and keep quiet?
Alcibiades. To the pilot.
Socrates. Therefore concerning the things you do not know, you do not wander, provided you know that you do not know them?
Alcibiades. It seems I do not.
Socrates. Do you then perceive that errors in action are also because of this ignorance—the ignorance of one who does not know thinking that he knows?
Alcibiades. How do you mean this again?
Socrates. We attempt to act, do we not, whenever we think we know what we are doing?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. But whenever people do not think they know, do they hand it over to others?
Alcibiades. How could they not?
Socrates. Do not such people among the ignorant live without error because of leaving these things to others?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Who then are those who err? For surely they are not those who know.
Alcibiades. No, indeed.

div.head: Section 118
div.p: Socrates. And since it is neither those who know, nor those among the ignorant who know that they do not know, are there any others left besides those who do not know, but think they know?
Alcibiades. No, only these.
Socrates. Is this ignorance then the cause of bad things, and the most reproachful stupidity?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And when it concerns the greatest things, is it then most harmful and most base?
Alcibiades. By far.
Socrates. What then? Can you name greater things than the just, the beautiful, the good, and the advantageous?
Alcibiades. No, indeed.
Socrates. Is it not concerning these that you say you are wandering?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And if you are wandering, is it not clear from what has preceded that not only are you ignorant of the greatest things, but also, not knowing them, you think you know them?
Alcibiades. It is likely.

Socrates. Alas then, Alcibiades, what a state you have suffered! I hesitate to name it, but nevertheless, since we are alone, it must be said. You are living with stupidity, my excellent friend, of the most extreme sort, as the argument accuses you and you accuse yourself. That is why you are rushing toward political affairs before being educated. And you are not the only one who has suffered this, but also the many who manage the affairs of this city, except a few and perhaps your guardian Pericles.

Alcibiades. It is said, at any rate, Socrates, that he did not become wise spontaneously, but by associating with many wise men, including Pythoclides and Anaxagoras; and even now at his age he associates with Damon for this very reason.

Socrates. What then? Have you ever seen anyone wise in anything who was unable to make someone else wise in the same things as himself? Just as the one who taught you your letters was himself wise and made you and anyone else he wished wise; isn't that so?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And you, having learned from him, will you also be able to teach another?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And the lyre-player and the physical trainer in the same way?
Alcibiades. Very much so.
Socrates. For this is surely a good proof of those who know anything that they know it, whenever they are also able to show another to be knowing.
Alcibiades. It seems so to me.
Socrates. What then? Can you say whom Pericles made wise, starting with his sons?
Alcibiades. What if the two sons of Pericles were foolish, Socrates?
Socrates. Then what about Clinias, your brother?
Alcibiades. Why would you mention Clinias, a madman?
Socrates. Well then, since Clinias is mad, and the two sons of Pericles were foolish, what cause shall we assign to him for overlooking you when you are in such a condition?
Alcibiades. I suppose I am the cause by not paying attention.

div.head: Section 119
div.p: Socrates. But tell me of any other Athenian or foreigner, slave or free, who has the reputation of having become wiser through association with Pericles, just as I can tell you that through association with Zeno, Pythodorus the son of Isolochus and Callias the son of Calliades each paid Zeno a hundred minas and became wise and eminent.
Alcibiades. But by Zeus, I cannot.
Socrates. Very well; what then do you intend concerning yourself? Whether to remain as you are now, or to take some care of yourself?

Alcibiades. It is a matter for common deliberation, Socrates. And yet I understand what you say and I agree; for it seems to me that those who manage the affairs of the city, with a few exceptions, are uneducated.
Socrates. What then follows from this?

Alcibiades. If they happened to be educated, one who attempted to contend with them would have to go having learned and practiced, as against athletes; but now, since these men have come to the affairs of the city being in an amateurish state, why is it necessary to practice and take the trouble to learn? For I know well that I shall surpass them very much by nature alone.
Socrates. Alas, my excellent friend, what a thing you have said! How unworthy of your appearance and of the other things that belong to you.
Alcibiades. Why especially, and to what end do you say this, Socrates?
Socrates. I am indignant both on your behalf and on behalf of my own love.
Alcibiades. Why is that?
Socrates. If you have deemed your contest to be against the men here.
Alcibiades. But against whom else should it be?
Socrates. Is this a worthy thing even to ask for a man who considers himself to be high-minded?
Alcibiades. How do you mean? Is my contest not against these men?

Socrates. But even if you intended to steer a trireme that was about to fight a naval battle, would it be enough for you to be the best at steering among your fellow sailors, or would you think that these things must be presupposed, and you would look to your true opponents, rather than as you do now to your fellow combatants? For surely you must surpass them by so much that they do not deem it fit to contend against you, but having been despised by you they fight alongside you against the enemy, if indeed you intend in truth to show forth some noble deed worthy both of yourself and of the city.
Alcibiades. But I do indeed intend to.

Socrates. Then it is altogether worthy for you to be content if you are better than the soldiers, and not to look toward the commanders of the adversaries to see if you have ever become better than them, examining and practicing against them.

div.head: Section 120
div.p: Alcibiades. Who are these you speak of, Socrates?
Socrates. Do you not know that our city is at war with the Lacedaemonians and with the Great King at all times?
Alcibiades. You speak the truth.

Socrates. Therefore if you intend to be the leader of this city, would you not be thinking correctly if you thought that your contest was against the kings of the Lacedaemonians and the king of the Persians?
Alcibiades. You are likely to speak the truth.

Socrates. No, my good friend, but you must look to Midias the quail-striker and others like him—who attempt to manage the affairs of the city while still having, as the women would say, the slave's hair in their souls due to lack of culture, and not yet having cast it off, but still acting like barbarians they have come to flatter the city but not to rule it—you must look to these men, as I say, and neglect yourself, and neither learn as much as pertains to learning, being about to fight such a great contest, nor practice as much as requires practice, and having prepared every preparation in this way go to the affairs of the city.
Alcibiades. But, Socrates, you seem to me to speak the truth, yet I think the generals of the Lacedaemonians and the king of the Persians do not differ from the rest.
Socrates. But, my excellent friend, consider what sort of opinion this is that you hold.
Alcibiades. Concerning what?
Socrates. First, in which way do you think you would take more care of yourself, fearing them and thinking them formidable, or not?
Alcibiades. Clearly if I thought them formidable.
Socrates. Do you then think you would suffer any harm by taking care of yourself?
Alcibiades. By no means, but I would even benefit greatly.
Socrates. Therefore this opinion has this one great evil.
Alcibiades. You speak the truth.
Socrates. Secondly, then, consider from probabilities that it is also false.
Alcibiades. How so?
Socrates. Is it probable that better natures are born in noble families or not?
Alcibiades. Clearly in noble ones.
Socrates. And do not those who are well born, if they are also well nurtured, thus become perfect with respect to virtue?
Alcibiades. Necessarily.

Socrates. Let us consider then, comparing their conditions with ours, first whether the kings of the Lacedaemonians and Persians seem to be of baser families. Or do we not know that the former are descendants of Heracles, and the latter of Achaemenes, and the family of Heracles and that of Achaemenes trace back to Perseus, the son of Zeus?

div.head: Section 121
div.p: Alcibiades. And ours, Socrates, traces back to Eurysaces, and that of Eurysaces to Zeus.

Socrates. And ours, my noble Alcibiades, to Daedalus, and Daedalus to Hephaestus, the son of Zeus. But their lines, beginning from these, have been kings from kings down to Zeus, the one of Argos and Lacedaemon, the other of Persia continuously, and often of Asia as well, just as now; while we are ourselves private citizens and so were our fathers. And if you had to show off your ancestors and the homeland of Eurysaces, Salamis, or that of Aeacus even before him, Aegina, to Artaxerxes the son of Xerxes, how much laughter do you think you would incur? But see lest we are inferior to the men not only in the bulk of our birth but also in our other upbringing. Or have you not perceived how great are the advantages belonging to the kings of the Lacedaemonians, whose wives are publicly guarded by the ephors, so that as far as possible it may not escape notice if a king is born from someone other than the Heraclidae? And the Persian king surpasses so much that no one even holds a suspicion that the king could be born from anyone but the king himself; therefore the king's wife is not guarded except by fear. And when the eldest son is born, to whom the rule belongs, first all those in the kingdom over whom he rules celebrate, and then for the rest of time on this day all Asia sacrifices and celebrates the king's birthday; but when we are born, as the comic poet says, not even the neighbors notice it very much, Alcibiades. After this the child is nurtured, not by a woman nurse of little worth, but by those eunuchs who seem to be the best around the king; to whom it is assigned both to take care of the newborn in other respects, and to contrive how he will be as beautiful as possible, molding and straightening the child's limbs; and doing these things they are held in great honor. And when the boys become seven years old, they go to the horses and to their teachers, and they begin to go on hunts. And when the boy becomes twice seven years old, those whom they call the royal tutors take him over; and these are four chosen men reputed to be the best among the Persians in their prime, the wisest and the most just and the most moderate and the most courageous.

div.head: Section 122
div.p:
Socrates. Of these, the first teaches the magic of Zoroaster, the son of Horomazes—and this is the worship of the gods—and he also teaches the duties of a king; the most just teaches him to be truthful throughout his whole life; the most moderate teaches him not to be mastered by a single one of the pleasures, so that he may become accustomed to being free and truly a king, ruling first the things within himself and not being a slave to them; and the most courageous prepares him to be fearless and without dread, since whenever he feels fear he is a slave. But for you, Alcibiades, Pericles set over you as a tutor the most useless of his servants because of old age, Zopyrus the Thracian. And I would go through the rest of the upbringing and education of your competitors, if it were not a long task and at the same time these things are sufficient to make clear the other things that follow from them. But of your birth, Alcibiades, and your upbringing and education, or that of any other Athenian, practically speaking no one cares, unless someone happens to be your lover. And if again you are willing to look to the wealth and luxuries and trailing garments of clothes and anointings with myrrh and the trailing crowds of attendants and the other refinements of the Persians, you would be ashamed of yourself, perceiving how much you fall short of them. And if again you will be willing to look to the moderation and orderliness and ease and even temper and high-mindedness and discipline and courage and endurance and love of toil and love of victory and love of honor of the Lacedaemonians, you would consider yourself a child in all such things. If again you pay attention to wealth and think you are something in this respect, let not this either remain unspoken by us, if somehow you may perceive where you stand. For in this respect, if you wish to look at the wealth of the Lacedaemonians, you will know that what is here falls far short of what is there; for as to the land they have, both their own and Messenia, no one here could dispute with them in size or virtue, nor again in the possession of slaves, both the others and the helots, nor indeed of horses, nor all the other flocks that graze throughout Messenia. But I let all these things go, yet in gold and silver there is not among all the Greeks as much as there is privately in Lacedaemon; for over many generations it enters there from all the Greeks, and often from the barbarians, but it goes out nowhere,
but simply according to the fable of Aesop which the fox told to the lion, while the tracks of the currency entering into Lacedaemon are clearly turned thither, nowhere could one see any going out.

div.head: Section 123
div.p: Socrates. So you must know well that both in gold and in silver those men are the wealthiest of the Greeks, and the king himself is the wealthiest among them; for from such sources the greatest and most numerous revenues come to the kings, and furthermore the royal tribute which the Lacedaemonians pay to the kings is not small. And the wealth of the Lacedaemonians is great compared to Greek wealth, but compared to the Persian wealth and that of their king it is nothing. Since I once heard a trustworthy man who had gone up to the king, who said that he passed through a very large and excellent region, nearly a day's journey, which the locals call the girdle of the king's wife; and there is another which is called the veil, and many other beautiful and good places separated for the adornment of the woman, and each of the places has a name from each of the adornments. So I think, if someone were to say to the king's mother, the wife of Xerxes, Amestris, that the son of Dinomache intends to array himself against your son, a woman whose adornment is perhaps worth fifty minas if very much, and her son has not even three hundred plethra of land in Erchia, she would wonder in what on earth this Alcibiades trusts when he intends to contend against Artaxerxes, and I think she would say that there is nothing else in which this man trusts when attempting this except care and wisdom; for these alone are worth speaking of among the Greeks. Since if she learned that this Alcibiades is now making the attempt first of all being not yet quite twenty years old, and secondly completely uneducated, and in addition to these things, when his lover tells him that he must first learn and take care of himself and practice before thus going to contend with the king, he is unwilling, but says that he is sufficient just as he is, I think she would marvel and ask: What on earth then is it in which the youth trusts? If then we were to say that it is in beauty and size and birth and wealth and the nature of his soul, she would consider us, Alcibiades, to be mad, looking at all such things among themselves.

div.head: Section 124
div.p: Socrates. And I think that even Lampido, the daughter of Leotychides, wife of Archidamus, and mother of Agis, who all became kings, would also marvel, looking at the things belonging to them, if you intend to contend with her son having been brought up so poorly. And yet does it not seem to be a shameful thing, if the wives of our enemies consider better concerning us what sort of men we must be to attempt against them, than we do concerning ourselves? But, my blessed friend, persuaded by me and by the inscription at Delphi, know yourself, that these are our adversaries, and not the ones you think; against whom we could not prevail over a single one in any other way, except by care and skill. If you are left behind in these, you will also be left behind in becoming renowned among both the Greeks and the barbarians, which I think you love as no one else loves anything else.
Alcibiades. What sort of care must I take, Socrates? Can you explain? For you most certainly seem to have spoken the truth.

Socrates. Yes; but indeed it is a matter of common deliberation in what way we would become the best possible. For I tell you I do not say that you must be educated, while I do not; for there is nothing in which I differ from you except in one thing.
Alcibiades. In what?
Socrates. My guardian is better and wiser than Pericles, your guardian.
Alcibiades. Who is this, Socrates?
Socrates. A god, Alcibiades, who did not allow me to converse with you before this day; trusting in whom I say that eminence will come to you through no one else but me.
Alcibiades. You are joking, Socrates.
Socrates. Perhaps; however, I speak the truth, that we need care, all men more or less, but we two very much indeed.
Alcibiades. That I do, you do not lie.
Socrates. Nor indeed that I do.
Alcibiades. What then should we do?
Socrates. We must not give up nor be soft, my comrade.
Alcibiades. No indeed, that is not fitting, Socrates.
Socrates. No, it is not, but we must consider together. Tell me then; for we say that we wish to become the best men. Is it not so?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Best in what virtue?
Alcibiades. Clearly the one that good men possess.
Socrates. Good at what?
Alcibiades. Clearly at managing affairs.
Socrates. What kind of affairs? Horsemanship?
Alcibiades. Certainly not.
Socrates. For we would go to horsemen for that?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. But do you mean naval affairs?
Alcibiades. No.
Socrates. For we would go to sailors for that?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. But what kind of affairs? Those which who manage?
Alcibiades. Those which the noble and good among the Athenians manage.

div.head: Section 125
div.p: Socrates. And by the noble and good do you mean the wise or the foolish?
Alcibiades. The wise.
Socrates. Therefore in whatever a man is wise, in that he is good?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And in whatever he is foolish, he is bad?
Alcibiades. How could he not be?
Socrates. Is the shoemaker then wise concerning the making of shoes?
Alcibiades. Very much so.
Socrates. So he is good in this?
Alcibiades. Good.
Socrates. What then? Is the shoemaker not foolish concerning the making of clothes?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. So he is bad at this?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Therefore the same man, by this argument at least, is both bad and good.
Alcibiades. It appears so.
Socrates. Do you then mean that good men are also bad?
Alcibiades. Certainly not.
Socrates. But who on earth do you mean by the good men?
Alcibiades. I mean those who are able to rule in the city.
Socrates. Not over horses, surely?
Alcibiades. Certainly not.
Socrates. But over men?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. When they are sick?
Alcibiades. No.
Socrates. When they are sailing?
Alcibiades. I do not mean that.
Socrates. When they are harvesting?
Alcibiades. No.
Socrates. But when they are doing nothing, or doing something?
Alcibiades. Doing something, I say.
Socrates. What? Try to make it clear to me too.
Alcibiades. Those who deal with themselves and associate with one another, just as we live in the cities.
Socrates. So you mean ruling over men who are associating with men?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Do you mean boatswains ruling over rowers?
Alcibiades. Certainly not.
Socrates. For that is the pilot's skill?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Do you mean ruling over flute-players, leading men in song and using chorus members?
Alcibiades. Certainly not.
Socrates. For that is again the chorus trainer's skill?
Alcibiades. Very much so.
Socrates. But what do you mean by being able to rule over men associating with men?
Alcibiades. I mean ruling over those sharing in the state and associating with one another, those in the city.
Socrates. What then is this art? Just as if I were to ask you again the same thing just now, what art makes one know how to rule over those sharing in a voyage?
Alcibiades. Pilotage.
Socrates. And over those sharing in song, as was just said, what knowledge makes one rule?
Alcibiades. The one you just mentioned, chorus training.
Socrates. What then? What do you call the knowledge of those sharing in the state?
Alcibiades. Good counsel, Socrates.
Socrates. What then? Does the knowledge of pilots seem to be bad counsel?
Alcibiades. Certainly not.
Socrates. But good counsel?

div.head: Section 126
div.p: Alcibiades. To me it does, at least towards the preservation of those sailing.
Socrates. You speak well. What then? The good counsel you speak of, what is it directed towards?
Alcibiades. Towards managing the city better and preserving it.

Socrates. And it is managed better and preserved by the presence or absence of what? Just as if you were to ask me, A body is managed better and preserved by the presence or absence of what? I would say that it is by the presence of health and the absence of disease. Do you not think so too?
Alcibiades. Yes.

Socrates. And if again you asked me, By the presence of what are eyes better? I would likewise say that it is by the presence of sight and the absence of blindness. And ears, with deafness departing and hearing entering, become better and are better cared for.
Alcibiades. Correct.
Socrates. What then? By the presence and absence of what does a city become better and is better cared for and managed?
Alcibiades. It seems to me, Socrates, that it is whenever friendship arises among them towards one another, and hatred and faction depart.
Socrates. By friendship do you mean agreement or disagreement?
Alcibiades. Agreement.
Socrates. Through what art, then, do cities agree concerning numbers?
Alcibiades. Through arithmetic.
Socrates. What about private individuals? Is it not through the same?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And each one with himself?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Through what art does each agree with himself concerning a span and a cubit, which is larger? Is it not through measuring?
Alcibiades. Of course.
Socrates. And private individuals with one another and cities?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. What then? Concerning weight, is it not the same way?
Alcibiades. I say it is.
Socrates. But the agreement you speak of, what is it and concerning what, and what art produces it? And is it the same for a city as for a private individual, both with himself and with another?
Alcibiades. It is likely, at any rate.
Socrates. What is it then? Do not grow weary in answering, but be eager to tell.
Alcibiades. I think it means the friendship and agreement which a father has loving his son, and a mother, and brother to brother, and wife to husband.
Socrates. Do you think then, Alcibiades, that a husband can agree with his wife concerning spinning, the one who does not know with the one who knows?
Alcibiades. Certainly not.
Socrates. Nor indeed should he; for this is a woman's learning.
Alcibiades. Yes.

div.head: Section 127
div.p: Socrates. What then? Could a woman agree with a man concerning heavy-armed fighting, not having learned it?
Alcibiades. Certainly not.
Socrates. For you would perhaps say that this is a man's learning.
Alcibiades. I would.
Socrates. Therefore there are women's learnings, and men's learnings, according to your argument.
Alcibiades. How could there not be?
Socrates. Therefore in these things at least there is no agreement between women and men.
Alcibiades. No.
Socrates. Nor indeed friendship, if friendship was agreement.
Alcibiades. It appears not.
Socrates. So insofar as women do their own things, they are not loved by their husbands.
Alcibiades. It seems not.
Socrates. Nor indeed are husbands by their wives insofar as they do their own things.
Alcibiades. No.
Socrates. Therefore cities are not well inhabited in this way, whenever each does their own things?
Alcibiades. I think they are, Socrates.
Socrates. How do you mean, when friendship is not present, the presence of which we said makes cities well inhabited, but otherwise not?
Alcibiades. But it seems to me that friendship arises in them precisely according to this, that each does their own things.

Socrates. It did not just now; but how do you say it again now? Does friendship arise without agreement arising? Or is it possible for agreement to arise concerning things about which some know and others do not?
Alcibiades. Impossible.
Socrates. And do they do just things or unjust things, whenever each does their own things?
Alcibiades. Just things; how could they not?
Socrates. So when the citizens do just things in the city, does friendship not arise among them towards one another?
Alcibiades. It again seems to me to be necessary, Socrates.

Socrates. What on earth then do you mean by the friendship or agreement concerning which we must be wise and of good counsel, in order that we may be good men? For I am unable to learn what it is or among whom it exists; for sometimes it appears to be present in the same people, and sometimes not, according to your argument.
Alcibiades. But by the gods, Socrates, I do not even know myself what I am saying, but I risk having for a long time been in a most shameful state without realizing it.

Socrates. But one must have courage. For if you had perceived you were suffering this at fifty years old, it would have been difficult for you to take care of yourself; but now the age you are at is the very one in which one must perceive this.
Alcibiades. What then must one who perceives it do, Socrates?
Socrates. Answer the questions asked, Alcibiades; and if you do this, if god wills, if one must trust my divination at all, both you and I shall be in a better state.
Alcibiades. This shall be, as far as my answering is concerned.

div.head: Section 128
div.p: Socrates. Come then, what is it to take care of oneself—lest perhaps we escape notice not taking care of ourselves, but thinking we do—and when does a man do it? Does he take care of himself whenever he takes care of the things belonging to him?
Alcibiades. To me at least it seems so.
Socrates. What then? When does a man take care of his feet? Is it whenever he takes care of the things that belong to the feet?
Alcibiades. I do not understand.
Socrates. Do you call something belonging to the hand? Like a ring, would you say it belongs to any other part of a man than the finger?
Alcibiades. Certainly not.
Socrates. And a shoe belonging to the foot in the same way?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And clothes and coverings of the rest of the body similarly?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. So whenever we take care of shoes, do we then take care of feet?
Alcibiades. I do not quite understand, Socrates.
Socrates. What then, Alcibiades? Do you call it taking proper care of any thing whatsoever?
Alcibiades. I do.
Socrates. Therefore whenever someone makes something better, do you call that proper care?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. What art then makes shoes better?
Alcibiades. Shoemaking.
Socrates. So by shoemaking we take care of shoes?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And also of the foot by shoemaking? Or by that art with which we make feet better?
Alcibiades. By that one.
Socrates. And do we not make feet better by the same art as the rest of the body?
Alcibiades. It seems so to me.
Socrates. And is this not gymnastics?
Alcibiades. Especially so.
Socrates. By gymnastics then we take care of the foot, and by shoemaking we take care of the things belonging to the foot?
Alcibiades. Very much so.
Socrates. And by gymnastics of the hands, but by ring-engraving of the things belonging to the hand?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And by gymnastics of the body, but by weaving and the other arts of the things belonging to the body?
Alcibiades. Absolutely.
Socrates. Therefore by one art we take care of each thing itself, and by another of the things belonging to it.
Alcibiades. It appears so.
Socrates. Therefore whenever you take care of the things belonging to yourself, you are not taking care of yourself.
Alcibiades. By no means.
Socrates. For it is not the same art, as it seems, by which one would take care of himself and of the things belonging to himself.
Alcibiades. It appears not.
Socrates. Come then, by what art on earth could we take care of ourselves?
Alcibiades. I am unable to say.
Socrates. But this much at least has been agreed, that it is not by the art which would make any of our possessions better, but the one which makes ourselves better?
Alcibiades. You speak the truth.
Socrates. Would we then ever know what art makes a shoe better, not knowing a shoe?
Alcibiades. Impossible.
Socrates. Nor indeed what art makes rings better, being ignorant of a ring.
Alcibiades. True.
Socrates. What then? What art makes a man himself better, could we ever know it being ignorant of what on earth we ourselves are?

div.head: Section 129
div.p: Alcibiades. Impossible.
Socrates. Does it then happen to be easy to know oneself, and was it some simpleton who dedicated this in the temple at Pytho, or is it something difficult and not for everyone?
Alcibiades. To me, Socrates, it has often seemed to be for everyone, and often extremely difficult.
Socrates. But, Alcibiades, whether it is easy or not, nevertheless it stands thus for us: knowing it we might quickly know the care of ourselves, but being ignorant of it, never.
Alcibiades. That is so.
Socrates. Come then, in what way might itself be found? For thus we might perhaps find what on earth we ourselves are, but still being in ignorance of this we surely cannot.
Alcibiades. You speak correctly.
Socrates. Hold on then, by Zeus. With whom are you conversing now? Is it anyone else but me?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And I with you?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Then Socrates is the one conversing?
Alcibiades. Very much so.
Socrates. And Alcibiades is the one listening?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Therefore Socrates converses using speech?
Alcibiades. Of course.
Socrates. And you call conversing and using speech the same thing, I suppose.
Alcibiades. Very much so.
Socrates. But the one using and what he uses are not different things?
Alcibiades. How do you mean?
Socrates. Just as a shoemaker cuts with a knife and an awl and other tools.
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Is not the one cutting and using different from the things he uses to cut?
Alcibiades. How could he not be?
Socrates. And in this way also the things with which the lyre-player plays the lyre and the lyre-player himself would be different?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. This then is what I was asking just now, whether the one using and what he uses always seem to be different.
Alcibiades. They do.
Socrates. What then shall we say of the shoemaker? Does he cut with tools only or also with his hands?
Alcibiades. With his hands too.
Socrates. Therefore he uses these as well?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And does he also use his eyes when shoemaking?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And do we agree that the one using and what he uses are different?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Therefore the shoemaker and lyre-player are different from the hands and eyes with which they work?
Alcibiades. It appears so.
Socrates. Does not a man also use his whole body?
Alcibiades. Very much so.
Socrates. And the one using and what he uses were different?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Therefore a man is different from his own body?
Alcibiades. It seems so.
Socrates. What on earth then is the man?
Alcibiades. I am unable to say.
Socrates. But you are able, that it is the thing which uses the body.
Alcibiades. Yes.

div.head: Section 130
div.p: Socrates. Does anything else use it but the soul?
Alcibiades. Nothing else.
Socrates. By ruling it?
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. And indeed I think no one would think otherwise about this.
Alcibiades. About what?
Socrates. That man is nothing else but one of three things.
Alcibiades. What three?
Socrates. Soul or body or both together, this whole thing.
Alcibiades. Of course.
Socrates. But did we not agree that the thing ruling the body is the man?
Alcibiades. We agreed.
Socrates. Does the body then rule itself?
Alcibiades. By no means.
Socrates. For we said it is ruled.
Alcibiades. Yes.
Socrates. Then this would not be what we are seeking.
Alcibiades. It seems not.
Socrates. But does the combination of both rule the body, and is this the man?
Alcibiades. Perhaps indeed.
Socrates. Least of all; for if one of the two does not share in ruling, there is surely no way that the combination rules.
Alcibiades. Correct.
Socrates. But since neither the body nor the combination is the man, it remains I think either that he is nothing, or if he is anything, the man happens to be nothing else than soul.
Alcibiades. Absolutely.
Socrates. Is it then necessary to demonstrate to you more clearly that the soul is the man?
Alcibiades. By Zeus, it seems to me to be sufficient.
Socrates. If it is not exact but moderate, it is sufficient for us; for we shall know it exactly then, whenever we find that which we just passed over because it required much consideration.
Alcibiades. What is that?

Socrates. That which was said somehow just now, that we must first consider itself; but now instead of itself we have considered what each thing itself is. And perhaps it will suffice; for we could hardly say that anything is more properly ourselves than the soul.
Alcibiades. Certainly not.
Socrates. Therefore is it well to believe thus, that you and I converse with one another using arguments, soul to soul?
Alcibiades. Very much so.

Socrates. This then was what we also said a little before, that Socrates converses with Alcibiades using speech, making arguments not to your face, as it seems, but to Alcibiades; and this is the soul.
Alcibiades. It seems so to me.
Socrates. Therefore the one enjoining to know oneself commands us to recognize the soul.
